pr_body:
Takes a list of CPUs and has the same syntax as a list of CPUs for `CPUAffinity=` option or special "all" value which will include all available CPUs in the mask. Currently, this will set CPU mask to all `rx` queue of matched device (if it has multiple queues).

The `/sys/class/net/<dev>/queues/rx-<n>/rps_cpus` only accept cpu bitmap mask in hexadecimal.

Fix: #30323

issue_context.title: Configure netdev RPS using systemd-networkd
issue_context.body:
### Component

systemd-networkd, systemd-udevd

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe

I asked this on systemd mailing list, the developer told me to submit a patch via GitHub. But I don't have the confidence to submit a patch here, I think it's better to create a feature request instead. So the more experienced developers could get started.

https://lists.freedesktop.org/archives/systemd-devel/2023-December/049724.html

In our environment, we use RPS (Receive Packet Steering) for load balancing and scaling. It's a kernel feature implemented a long time ago. You could visit the documentation at https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/scaling.html.

Currently, we manually do this after network interface is configured:
```shell
echo f > /sys/class/net/eth0/queues/rx-0/rps_cpus
```
where f is bitmap mask 1111, it means to utilize 4 cpus.

### Describe the solution you'd like

In the mailing list, Lennart suggested this can be added to `.link` files. Perhaps like this:
```ini
[Match]
Type=ether

[Link]
ReceivePacketSteeringCPUMask=f
```
I am not really sure if the values must be in bitmap mask or can be comma separated like `CPUAffinity`.

To verify you could read:
```shell
 cat /sys/class/net/eth0/queues/rx-0/rps_cpus
```

The general path is:
```
/sys/class/net/<dev>/queues/rx-<n>/rps_cpus
```
The number of queues depends on the hardware. Most our hardwares only have single queue.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

I could use `networkd-dispatcher` or `networkd-broker` to execute a script after the interface is configured. That's my current workaround.

### The systemd version you checked that didn't have the feature you are asking for

254

Hmm... If the setting is not specified, RPS is unchanged, and the kernel default is that RPS is disabled.
If `all` is specified, RPS is enabled with all CPUs. But, that's mostly equivalent to disabling RPS, unless CPUs will be hot plugged later. So, setting `all` is mostly meaningless.
Do you have any specific usecases of `all`? If not, please drop it.

> If `all` is specified, RPS is enabled with all CPUs. But, that's mostly equivalent to disabling RPS.

I think that wouldn't be equivalent, from the kernel docs, suggested that enabling all CPUs is a valid use case.

> For a single queue device, a typical RPS configuration would be to set the rps_cpus to the CPUs in the same memory domain of the interrupting CPU. If NUMA locality is not an issue, this could also be **all CPUs** in the system. 

> Do you have any specific usecases of `all`?

We use RPS to prevent swapped frame caused by OOO (out of order) in our devices with SMP CPUs (4 core).
Interesting.
